newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: HIGH RATES SPELL SCROOGE CHRISTMAS IN S.AFRICA.
newsitem.headline: HIGH RATES SPELL SCROOGE CHRISTMAS IN S.AFRICA.

text.p: South Africa's latest interest rate hike has cast a pall over Christmas shoppers and darkened the economic outlook for 1997, in a bitter reversal of prospects 12 months ago.
This time last year, an upbeat South Africa was looking forward to rate cuts and a surge in economic growth and investment, funded by record foreign capital inflows.

Today the key Bank rate stands two points higher than at the end of 1995, at 17 percent, and growth is slowing sharply as South Africans pay the price for the foreign exchange market's attack on the rand.
Nedcor, one of the country's top four banks, said on Friday it was revising its forecast for economic growth in 1997 down to two percent from 2.2 percent before Wednesday night's rate hike.
Other economists also said they were adjusting downwards.

"We are now talking about a somewhat deeper, a somewhat more prolonged downswing and bottoming out phase in the business cycle," said Pieter Laubscher of the University of Stellenbosch's Bureau for Economic Research (BER).

Punishing interest rates -- among the world's highest after allowing for an inflation rate of nine percent -- may finally allow central bank governor Chris Stals to defeat a runaway credit boom, even permitting a rate cut within six months or so.
But the price will be high on an already flagging economy unable to support the hundreds of thousands of youngsters entering the job market each year.
In June, the government outlined a macro-economic plan designed to double growth a year by 2000, from 3.3 percent in 1995 and an estimated three percent this year.
The aim is create 400,000 new jobs a year and finally dent an unemployment rate affecting a third of the workforce.
But key elements of the strategy already appear under threat with official projections for 1997 looking over-optimistic.
The growth, employment and redistribution document (known as GEAR) projects gross domestic product rising 2.9 percent in 1997 and 3.8 in 1998, en route to an eventual 6.1 percent growth in 2000.

A key proviso of these projections, however, is a cut in interest rates, something Stals has been unable to deliver in the face of persistent attacks on the rand which have stoked inflation, exposed balance of payment problems and sliced into reserves.
Economists are still hopeful that interest rates will come down again in 1997 as the trade balance improves further on the back of an export boom engendered by the weak rand.
But in the meantime the outlook remains grim for companies, many of whom were already warning about the impact of flagging demand for their goods before the latest rate hike.

The pain will be felt especially in the consumer sector and stock analysts were predicting further pressure on share prices next week after heavy falls on Thursday following the rise in interest rates.
"For the man in the street this (rate hike) is the final straw in terms of forcing a cutback in consumption levels," said John Winship, managing director BOE Asset Management.
"The industrial board, particularly the consumer-based shares, will come under further pressure."

Stals said firm action was needed to keep the economy on track. "Unless this opportunity is grasped South Africa will have to face the tribulation of lower economic growth with higher inflation," he said on announcing his latest rate hike.
The economy was entering a period of consolidation which should help the rand stabilise, he said.
But for many South Africans it will not be a very festive Christmas.
